documents.abstract: Human performance often fails not because latent capacity is absent, but because access to high-functioning cognitive states is unstable under fatigue, distraction, overload, and pressure. This hypothesis paper proposes closed-loop cognitive state control—informally, supercognition —as a neuroengineering objective: rapid entry into, stabilization of, and recovery of an individual's highest available task-specific cognitive state. The framework treats cognition as a partially observable dynamical system whose latent states would be inferred from multimodal behavioral, physiological, contextual, and neural signals, and specifies a five-layer architecture comprising multimodal sensing, latent-state inference, predictive transition modeling, closed-loop intervention, and a longitudinal personal neural twin. The proposal is situated against existing closed-loop and neuroadaptive architectures, with an explicit statement of what is and is not new. The state ontology is given as a set of falsifiable assumptions rather than an intuitive taxonomy. Candidate computational implementations are specified for each layer, including hidden semi-Markov and switching state-space models, Bayesian and Kalman filtering, sequence models, hazard models, contextual bandits, model-predictive control, and offline reinforcement learning. The personal neural twin receives an operational specification covering its data requirements, update schedule, calibration and drift-monitoring criteria, and failure modes. Predictive and causal claims are separated, with the evidentiary requirements stated for each. The paper engages directly with the literature that challenges the framework's feasibility, including biomarker reliability, mixed neurofeedback findings, cross-task and cross-subject generalization failure, and the ecological-validity gap in wearable neurotechnology. Operational definitions, application scenarios, a validation protocol with power and diversity requirements, an expanded ethics and governance analysis, and a staged research roadmap are provided. No component of the architecture has been implemented or evaluated here: no simulation, clinical trial, or empirical efficacy claim is presented, and the validation programme described is prospective. The contribution is a falsifiable systems-engineering hypothesis for cognitive-state control.

Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through executable harnesses that govern tool use and feedback. Optimizing a harness for a fixed policy overlooks how its behavior changes during learning, while training a policy under a fixed harness leaves the interface that generates its training experience unchanged. This motivates adapting the harness throughout policy training. We introduce CoHARL, a population-based reinforcement learning framework that co-evolves a shared policy and a population of executable harnesses. The policy learns from rollouts across the population, and a proposer uses its execution traces to revise harness code during training. CoHARL achieves a 27.6% mean resolved rate on SWE-rebench, improving over harness-only search by 6.4 percentage points. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show gains in software engineering and terminal-based tasks. Under matched training budgets, CoHARL also outperforms searching for a harness once before RL and alternating policy updates with revisions to a single active harness.

The rapid integration of generative AI tools into spoken English instruction has produced measurable fluency and accuracy gains, but whether these are evenly distributed across the dimensions of communicative competence remains underexplored. This quasi-experimental study compares the Spiral Synergy Framework (SSF), a three-layer pedagogical sequence (AI Consolidation, Bridging Tasks, Interpersonal Activation), against conventional AI-integrated instruction in two intact Business English classes at a Chinese higher vocational college (experimental n = 36, control n = 34), using oral recordings at three time points scored on five competence dimensions, 15 weeks of classroom observation, and an intra-rater reliability check. The two classes differed significantly at baseline on the oral composite score and three of five dimensions (control higher), though not on CET-4 proficiency or questionnaire items. Because treatment is confounded with class membership and both classes received AI-assisted practice, findings are reported as associations rather than demonstrated causal effects. Linear mixed-effects models testing Group × Time interactions across five outcomes (four dimensions and the composite), corrected for multiple comparisons, identified one outcome - real-time responsiveness - on which the classes diverged: the experimental class maintained responsiveness across the semester while the control class declined despite its baseline advantage (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p = .029), a result that held under a cluster-robust sensitivity check. No corrected between-group difference was found for improvisation, coherence, naturalness, or the composite score; improvisation declined descriptively in both classes over the semester. Classroom observation data (experimental class only) document a recurring, non-monotonic cycle of AI-dependency reduction and rebound across 15 weeks. Intra-rater test-retest reliability of the oral-competence ratings was moderate to good (ICC = .67-.91), though this reflects a single rater familiar with participants rather than independent inter-rater agreement. Implications for multidimensional assessment, task sequencing, and cautious interpretation of AI-integrated curriculum research are discussed.

How do broader values shape whether people judge artificial intelligence (AI) as good or bad for humanity? This article analyzes provisional World Values Survey Wave 8 data from 40,960 respondents in 24 country samples using pooled and national prediction models, outcome-independent respondent profiles, and groups of countries. The analysis reveals a cross-country anchor: general optimism about science and technology is the strongest pooled predictor of favorable AI evaluation and recurs among the leading predictors in every national sample. Expert authority, education and information access, selected forms of trust, openness, and demographic position provide nationally distinctive patterns. Eleven value profiles formed without AI attitudes span 49.1% to 62.2% favorable evaluation. Most evaluative variation occurs within these profiles, making them useful contexts for identifying how the same values distinguish favorable from unfavorable evaluators in different social configurations. Institutional legitimacy, structural advantage, information connectedness, personal choice, redistribution, and openness differentiate evaluations in particular profiles. The same axis can relate differently to AI evaluation across profiles: secular reasoning has a significant positive association among secular moderate pluralists but a suggestive negative association among institution-trusting civic joiners. Together, the findings show that public receptivity to AI as technological change has a common predictive anchor but develops within plural configurations of resources, institutions, authority, openness, and social position. This distinction helps anticipate where generalized technological optimism is likely to travel and where AI deployment and governance will encounter context-specific sources of legitimacy or concern.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: LLM agents that answer questions and act on behalf of users must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees. Disagreement may correct a genuine error or may be an attempt at manipulation. Prior work shows that models frequently abandon correct answers when challenged by users, yet it remains unclear whether they distinguish correction from manipulation or merely differ in their propensity to concede. We examine this question across seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on the actions they take as customer-support agents whose policy permits account changes only for verified users. Simulated users push toward correct and incorrect answers with graded pressure. Following research on epistemic vigilance, the pressure either appeals to the source, such as claimed authority, or offers content the agent cannot verify, namely a cited source. Drawing on signal detection theory, we measure on a set of benchmark questions how much more readily each agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, separately from its overall propensity to concede. Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study, five models never violated the verification policy, including models that readily abandoned correct answers, so concession on answers did not predict violations of policy. Ministral 3B violated the policy mainly under claimed authority, and Ministral 8B reported changes it had not made. An instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence chiefly shifted propensity to concede rather than improving discrimination. Concession rates alone are therefore misleading, and agents should be evaluated on both their discrimination and the actions they take.

Large language model (LLM)-driven agents are emerging as a powerful new paradigm for solving complex problems. Despite the empirical success of these practices, a theoretical framework to understand and unify their macroscopic dynamics remains lacking. This paper proposes a method based on the least action principle to estimate the underlying generative directionality of LLMs embedded within agents. By experimentally measuring the transition probabilities between LLM-generated states, we report evidence consistent with a tendency toward detailed balance in LLM-generated transitions, indicating that LLM generation may not be achieved by generally learning rule sets and strategies, but rather by implicitly learning a class of underlying potential functions that may transcend different LLM architectures and prompt templates. To our knowledge, this provides an effective macroscopic description of LLM generative dynamics that does not depend on specific model details. This work is an attempt to establish a macroscopic dynamics theory of complex AI systems, aiming to elevate the study of AI agents from a collection of engineering practices to a science built on effective measurements that are predictable and quantifiable.

Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) are increasingly enabled by advances in automation, autonomy, network connectivity and shoreside support systems. These technologies create opportunities to offload tasks to Remote Operating Centers (ROCs), reduce and/or remove onboard crew, thus facilitating a wide variety of approaches for how ships are controlled and monitored in comparison to traditional shipping. This paper details a design case study of an ROC for an 8-meter diesel-electric uncrewed and autonomous-capable test ship operating in North Atlantic Canadian waters. A series of user-centered workshops and design iterations were implemented to redesign and refine the ROC physical work environment and Human-Machine Interfaces to better align with the goals and demands of shoreside operators. This work provides methodological and design contributions to MASS ROC development, while also creating a foundation for human-performance testing involving ROC operators and autonomous surface ships for the next phases of research and development.

Prior research suggests that vehicles with longer-wavelength or lighter colors are associated with faster perceived speeds compared to shorter-wavelength or darker colors, but TTC estimates were not measured. In the current study, participants viewed a simulated traffic scene in which a red or blue vehicle approached for 3 s and disappeared. Participants pressed a button when they believed the vehicle would reach their position. Red vehicles were judged to arrive sooner (TTC was underestimated) than blue vehicles (TTC was overestimated), but only when TTC was 4 s. Results suggest that vehicle color may be used as a heuristic cue to judge TTC when cognitive motion extrapolation demands are putatively higher.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being integrated into higher education, offering potential gains in efficiency and quality, yet there are concerns about its cognitive and behavioral consequences. This study surveyed 633 university students in Benin to examine factors associated with GenAI use and its academic, behavioral and psychological outcomes. Drawing on the Expectancy Value Theory and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), we used Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling to assess how Academic Workload, Time Pressure, and motivational sensitivities relate to GenAI use and its association with Academic Performance, Procrastination, and Self-Perceived Memory Decline. Results show that Academic Workload, Time Pressure, and motivational factors (Sensitivity to Rewards and Quality) were positively associated with GenAI use, which was widespread – more than 90% of students reporting use at least twice per week. GenAI use was positively associated with higher Academic Performance, but also with increased Procrastination and Self-Perceived Memory Decline. Contrary to prior research, age, gender, and education level were not significantly associated with GenAI use, reflecting the widespread GenAI adoption across student groups. These findings highlight GenAI’s dual role as both a potential performance-support tool and a mechanism of cognitive offloading, underscoring the need for balanced integration strategies that leverage AI-assisted efficiency while preserving meaningful cognitive engagement and mitigating risks associated with overreliance on AI tools.

documents.abstract: Innovation is increasingly important for organisations seeking to adapt to rapid economic changes and sustain competitiveness through effective human capital utilisation and employee creativity. In Malaysia, strengthening innovation outcomes aligns with the national aspiration to develop a knowledge and innovation-driven economy, as reflected in the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan (RMK13) 2026–2030. As key academic knowledge professionals, professors play an important role in knowledge creation, research and institutional innovation. However, empirical understanding of the personal resources and work-related mechanisms that foster innovative work behaviour (IWB) among professors in Malaysian private universities remains limited. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) Theory, this study examines the relationships of self-efficacy (SE) and intrinsic motivation (IM) with IWB and evaluates the mediating role of work engagement (WE). Using a quantitative research design and purposive sampling, data were collected from 205 professors across private universities in Malaysia and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4. The findings show that WE is positively and significantly associated with IWB. SE and IM are positively and significantly associated with WE and WE significantly mediates the relationships of both SE and IM with IWB. The findings contribute to Strategic Human Resource Management (SHRM) literature by highlighting WE as an important mechanism linking personal resources with IWB in the Malaysian higher education sector. Practically, the study provides insights for HR practitioners and institutional leaders to strengthen personal resources and work engagement, optimise talent management, and foster supportive workplace environments that promote academic innovation.

Scaling assessment in higher education faces two intertwined bottlenecks: the cognitive burden of authoring assessments and the inability to semantically evaluate open-ended responses, which together create a persistent feedback gap that hinders student learning outcomes. To address these challenges, we present Edhivo, an AI-native pedagogical platform that addresses both bottlenecks through a vertically integrated system for content delivery, assessment, and reporting. Edhivo employs a Dual-LLM pipeline: one model generates context-aware assessments for both multiple-choice and open-ended questions, from instructor-provided materials, while a second model performs multi-criteria, rubric-based evaluation of student responses, enabling near-instant qualitative feedback at multiple hierarchical levels. All AI interactions are source-grounded to reduce hallucination risk, and a Human-in-the-Loop review process preserves instructor authority. We demonstrate Edhivo's efficacy through a pilot deployment at Stony Brook University in a real classroom environment in 2026 spring, where it supports high-frequency assessment creation and evaluation for a cohort of 36 students throughout a full semester, significantly reducing authoring effort and feedback latency while enabling novel pedagogical designs centered on active learning.

documents.abstract: Higher distance education opens a wide range of opportunities for students with different socio-demographic backgrounds (e.g., age, gender, native language) and task-related skills (e.g., experience in scientific reading or online learning, previous degrees). Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL), where students work together in virtual groups, is a common teaching method in distance education. The current research investigates the consequences of stereotypes for targets and perceivers during the formation and collaboration phases in multi-attributionally diverse CSCL groups by systematically examining the individual level and the CSCL-group level. N = 2,023 students in 285 CSCL groups participated in a longitudinal field study in the introductory module of the BSc Psychology curriculum at a large European public distance teaching university. Analyses of multilevel models corresponding to pre-registered hypotheses replicated the findings of previous research that CSCL groups with high socio-demographic and high task-related diversity showed lower structural integration during collaboration. To explain this at-risk constellation for CSCL groups with highly diverse members, we investigated the role of being a target vs. perceiver of negative stereotypes within the group. Targets experiencing social identity threat reported a lower sense of belonging to the CSCL group and, consequently, lower motivation to initiate and maintain social relations with other group members. Moreover, targets generally reported higher social identity threat. Findings are discussed in terms of social-psychological approaches to microdynamics in CSCL groups and interventions to mitigate effects of diversity and stereotyping in higher distance education.

Generative AI (GenAI) offers opportunities for repeated practice and feedback in English language learning. However, how students participate in these learning activities requires further investigation. This study examined learning engagement profiles and their associations with GenAI use and speaking performance among 500 STEM master’s students in an AI-assisted ESAP speaking course at a Chinese university. Latent profile analysis used self-reported behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement scores collected in Week 15. Separate R3STEP models examined associations with self-reported weekly GenAI use frequency and average weekly online duration. BCH analyses compared posttest speaking performance across profiles while adjusting for pretest scores. Four profiles emerged: Low Engagement Profile (P1, 22.4%), High Engagement Profile (P2, 38.2%), Low Emotional Engagement Profile (P3, 24.0%), and Low Cognitive Engagement Profile (P4, 15.4%). Proportions were based on most likely assignments. After Holm correction, longer online duration was associated with higher odds of membership in P2, P3, and P4 relative to P1. More frequent GenAI use was associated with membership in P2 and P4 relative to P3. P2 had significantly higher baseline-adjusted overall speaking scores than all other profiles. These findings provide person-centered evidence of learner heterogeneity in AI-assisted ESAP. They highlight the value of considering multidimensional engagement configurations alongside GenAI use indicators when interpreting differences in speaking performance.

University students' psychological well-being is a critical public health concern, creating demand for digital interventions that are both safe and effective. Although conversational agents offer scalable support, existing usability heuristics cannot address complex affective dimensions such as emotional containment and clinical safety, revealing a gap in specialized design frameworks. To address this, the study introduces the “Affective Design Checklist,” a practical inspection tool for developing and auditing mental health conversational agents. Using Jabareen's conceptual framework analysis with a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 43 key articles, the instrument underwent a two-stage validation by a panel of ten experts, achieving a scale-level Content Validity Index (S-CVI/Ave) of 0.971, with near-unanimous agreement on ethical and regulatory dimensions. This research translates abstract bioethical and affective computing principles into actionable verification items, offering a specialized standard to ensure digital interventions are technically usable, affectively competent, and ethically aligned with student needs.

Abstract Artificial intelligence is typically linked to the learning platform, the diagnosis of skills and employment services, but the advantages of AI to workforce training are still not even as the skills acquired in the learning platform are not automatically available for use. There is already a significant amount of published work that discusses automation risk, as well as digital competencies and the role of AI in learning and development, but less comparative focus on the institutions that transform learning resources into recognised skills and employability through the operation and use of AI enabled and/or AI relevant learning environments. By designing it around the theoretically motivated Capability Approach of Sen, this study analyzed SkillsFuture Singapore and the European Digital Skills and Jobs Coalition and India’s National Career Service using a qualitative comparative documentary approach. Thematic analysis was performed using secondary data such as all documents of platforms, official documents, intergovernmental document and peer-reviewed literature, which were publicly available and interpreted each case one by one as a documentary thematic analysis. It suggests that the strength of workforce-learning ecosystems emerges when combined with trying to make digital accessible, within an affordable context, with digital skills, counselling, assisted access, language-sensitive design, recognition by employers, transparency in governance, and evidence of outcomes. With Singapore demonstrating coordinated lifelong learning, Europe demonstrates the good and bad of mobilising digital skills across multiple stakeholders and levels and India helps to show how to apply the reach of platforms to employment-related skills inclusion at large scale. The analysis of the study presents a framework for capability conversion, which attempts to simultaneously analyze the AI-relevant workforce's learning, even though the mere presence of the platform does not guarantee it is effective. The shocks are not "user" shocks or "platform-internal" shocks because of the documentary nature of the evidence, which leaves room for analytical interpretations of the findings as more representative of outcomes in the labour market rather than causal interpretations.

Fostering more self-determined forms of motivation in students remains a key challenge in education. According to self-determination theory (SDT), educational environments supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness enhance more autonomous forms of motivation. Music education in collaborative, learner-centered formats may provide such conditions. This study investigates whether participation in learner-centered orchestral training is associated with changes in children's general academic motivation.The study involved 113 children aged 8–10 years. Half joined a three-month orchestral program emphasizing active participation, peer collaboration, and public performance. The other half formed a control group with no music training. Motivation was assessed pre- and post-training using the Academic Self-Regulation Questionnaire.Children in the music group showed a greater reduction in external regulation compared to the control group. For intrinsic motivation, a descriptive trend toward improvement was observed in the music group relative to the control group, although the Group x Time interaction did not reach statistical significance.These findings suggest that learner-centered orchestral training may support a shift towards more self-determined forms of motivation, primarily through reduced external regulation.

ENGLISH This critical conceptual essay examines how to distinguish a proposed AI-assisted scientific discovery from its validation, the documented contributions of participants, and responsibility for communicating the result. It develops a four-register framework covering the scientific claim, the standard of evidence attained, the provenance of contributions, and communication responsibility. Published examples illustrate why generating hypotheses or computational results is not, by itself, equivalent to validating all claims made about them. The essay reports no original experiment or systematic review; the proposed framework has not been empirically validated. This record contains the complete English and Spanish editions, Version 1.0. ESPAÑOL Este ensayo crítico y conceptual examina cómo distinguir una propuesta de descubrimiento científico asistido por IA de su validación, las contribuciones documentadas de sus participantes y la responsabilidad de comunicar el resultado. Desarrolla un marco de cuatro registros: afirmación científica, estándar de prueba alcanzado, procedencia de las contribuciones y responsabilidad comunicativa. Los ejemplos publicados ilustran por qué generar hipótesis o resultados computacionales no equivale por sí solo a validar todas las afirmaciones derivadas de ellos. No presenta experimentos originales ni una revisión sistemática; el marco propuesto todavía no ha sido validado empíricamente. Este registro contiene las ediciones completas en inglés y español, versión 1.0.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This reflective article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents configured as educational tutors in secondary education. Based on a rigorous review of meta-analyses, international case studies, and specialized academic literature, it explores the conceptual foundations of intelligent tutoring and contemporary models of digital pedagogy. It examines real-world applications of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), their benefits in terms of learning personalization, immediate feedback, student autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Likewise, ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias, risks of dehumanizing educational processes, and vulnerabilities related to data privacy are identified. Finally, pedagogical guidelines are presented for the ethical and effective integration of AI agents in school settings, emphasizing teacher training, student-centered design, and continuous educational impact assessment.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $τ$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

Abstract Purpose: Software projects are increasingly using repository-level governance artifacts, such as \texttt{CLAUDE.md} and \texttt{AGENTS.md}, to communicate project-specific guidance to AI coding agents. Although these artifacts have become an important mechanism for governing AI coding agents, little is known about the governance practices and liabilities they encode, or whether their observable characteristics are consistent with organizational governance capability. Method: To examine these questions, we conducted an exploratory sequential mixed-methods study of 555 AI agent governance artifacts collected from public GitHub repositories. Using Socio-Technical Grounded Theory for Data Analysis (STGT4DA), we developed taxonomies of governance practices and governance liabilities, which were converted into a structured codebook for LLM-based classification. The codebook was evaluated against manually coded reference labels and applied to the corpus to examine whether these artifacts exhibit observable characteristics theoretically associated with organizational governance capability. Results: The findings reveal that these artifacts primarily emphasize knowledge transfer, process guidance, and coding standards, whereas explicit oversight mechanisms, such as human approval gates, remain comparatively limited. The analysis also identifies recurring governance liabilities, most commonly vague instructions (36%) and fragmentation debt (35%). We found no systematic association between the governance observed in the artifacts and the repository maturity indicators examined in this study, nor did governance vary systematically across the application domains examined as broad proxies for potential operational consequences. The artifacts also showed limited evidence of characteristics associated with institutionalized governance, particularly regarding accountability mechanisms, coherence between governance content and governance quality, and project-specific adaptation. Conclusion: This study provides an empirical investigation of repository-level AI agent governance from an organizational capability perspective. By examining governance artifacts according to the governance functions they perform rather than solely the information they contain, the study develops taxonomies of governance practices and liabilities and an evaluated LLM-based classification approach for systematically characterizing AI agent governance in research and practice.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to examine how EFL learners' trust in AI feedback, AI-related anxiety, and AI literacy relate to their engagement with, and uptake of, AI-mediated written corrective feedback. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined survey data from 300 university EFL learners, analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), with follow-up semi-structured interviews (n = 16); the structural model explained 48% of the variance in feedback uptake. AI literacy positively predicted trust (β = .46) and negatively predicted anxiety (β = -.39); trust was the strongest positive predictor of both engagement (β = .41) and uptake (β = .44), while anxiety exerted smaller negative effects. A cluster analysis identified three learner profiles - Confident Collaborators, Anxious Verifiers, and Detached Low-Literacy Users. Because anxiety was measured at three points across the period of AI-mediated collaboration, change over time was also examined: a repeated-measures ANOVA showed AI anxiety declining significantly across the three waves (partial η² = .18), and a latent growth curve model showed that higher AI literacy and higher trust each predicted a steeper decline. The qualitative findings showed that learners did not accept AI feedback uncritically but practised calibrated trust, verifying machine feedback against teachers and peers, and that AI literacy functioned as a regulating resource that tempered both over-reliance and anxiety. On this basis the study proposes a Calibrated Trust Framework for AI-mediated assessment, in which AI literacy supports calibrated trust, calibrated trust drives engagement, and engagement converts into uptake. The study advances a learner-centred account of human-AI collaboration in language assessment and argues that AI literacy, rather than tool sophistication alone, is central to responsible, pedagogically meaningful, AI-mediated assessment. Implications for assessment design, teacher education, and ethical practice are discussed.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational life, yet whether and how this technology benefits employees remains poorly understood, particularly in emerging economies where digital transformation is proceeding rapidly but unevenly. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and Psychological Empowerment Theory, this study examines how organizational AI capability relates to employee performance and engagement and asks whether psychological empowerment channels this relationship and whether digital organizational culture strengthens or weakens it. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of 387 employees across 42 organizations in Egypt spanning the banking, telecommunications, healthcare, manufacturing, and retail sectors, and were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling with bootstrapped mediation tests and multi-group comparisons. AI capability was positively associated with both employee performance and engagement, and employee empowerment partially mediated these relationships, indicating that AI's benefits for employees flow substantially through employees' sense of autonomy, competence, and impact rather than through technology alone. Digital organizational culture moderated this pathway: the AI capability-to-empowerment relationship was roughly twice as strong in organizations with a well-developed digital culture as in those without one. These findings extend the Resource-Based View to the individual level, position empowerment as a key psychological mechanism linking organizational AI resources to human outcomes and demonstrate that AI's human benefits are culturally and organizationally contingent rather than automatic. The results contribute emerging-economy evidence to a literature dominated by developed-country studies and offer practical guidance for organizations seeking to deploy AI in ways that empower, rather than sideline, their workforce.

Abstract UK agriculture is facing an acute labour shortage, particularly on small farms where unpredictable and unstructured environments make automation difficult. Although robotic systems offer promising solutions, fully autonomous approaches remain costly and complex to implement. Human--Robot Collaboration provides a more practical alternative by combining human judgement with robotic assistance. This study investigates how digital twin-based simulation platforms can be designed to effectively model and optimise collaboration between humans and robots in complex agricultural settings. It also examines the performance trade-offs in vision and gesture-based collaboration systems, focusing on the balance between speed, accuracy and robustness, and explores the safety challenges related to recognising human intent and ensuring safe adaptive behaviour.To address these issues, a digital twin framework was constructed using the NVIDIA Omniverse platform, enabling the simulation of collaborative agricultural scenarios. The virtual testbed includes dynamic farm layouts, human models, and mobile robots equipped with RGB and LiDAR sensors to interpret gestures and actions with AI and a Vision-Language Model. Experimental results show high human detection accuracy (intersection over union up to 97%) and reliable robot responses to human guidance. This research presents the first virtual environment in agriculture that integrates human factors and intelligent robotic reasoning. The proposed framework provides a scalable, low-risk approach for developing, testing and optimising collaborative robotic systems, supporting wider adoption of intelligent automation in the farming sector.

The written paper has long stood in as proof of work: a fluent, well-structured manuscript was taken as evidence that good research lay behind it. Generative AI has broken that link. Polished manuscripts now cost nothing to produce, submissions are outgrowing what reviewers can absorb, and venues are turning to AI for help. The logical endpoint is a loop where AI writes the papers and AI reviews them. We argue that this loop is survivable, but only if it is given a reward function, and that human reviewing effort should become that reward function. We propose that submissions should consist of a 1500-word brief plus an unlimited, machine-verifiable appendix. Human reviewers judge whether a pursuit is worthwhile, models verify the experimental record in the appendix, and human curation decides where the field goes next.

The original roots of the information society (jōhō shakai) are clearly Japanese and date back to the year 1963. The concept was developed in the context of a private study group circle spearheaded by the anthropologist Umesao Tadao, including members like the science fiction writer Komatsu Sakyō and the futurologist Hayashi Yūjirō. Drawing on the methodology of science and technology studies (STS), I will show how the ideological narrative underlying Umesao’s original theory on the information industries was condensed into a sociotechnical imaginary (STI) in the years from 1963 to the end of the 1970s. This article explains why the narrative was so successful and how the Expo 1970 in Osaka served as a showcase for the public performance and stabilization of the STI. The article argues that this contributed to its lasting impact on the way in which Japanese technofutures were imagined, based on the premise of a techno-centered society.

The modern Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) is undergoing a profound paradigm shift driven by the rapid maturation of generative artificial intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), and automated program synthesis engines. While historical transitions—from linear Waterfall models to Agile sprints and continuous DevOps pipelines—focused primarily on procedural orchestration and organizational agility, the integration of Artificial Intelligence introduces cognitive automation directly into the engineering fabric. This research paper presents an exhaustive empirical and methodological investigation into the impact of AI across the end-to-end SDLC, evaluating its tangible ramifications on developer productivity, cognitive workflow dynamics, code quality engineering, and enterprise security. Employing a rigorous triangulated mixed-methods research design, this study combines: (i) quantitative repository mining across 1,200,000 commits spanning 45 enterprise software projects; (ii) a controlled randomized quasi-experiment comprising N = 120 professional software engineers measuring task velocity and cognitive workload via the NASA-TLX inventory; and (iii) longitudinal static analysis tracking post-release defect density and Common Weakness Enumerations (CWE). Our findings demonstrate that AI assistance compresses coding lead times by 55.8% and accelerates developer flow states, yielding substantial improvements across DORA deployment frequency and change velocity metrics. However, ungoverned AI code generation introduces acute quality paradoxes, including a 19.4% surge in code churn, subtle logic regression risks, and elevated vulnerabilities in insecure deserialization and unverified package dependencies. To resolve this tension, we propose a multi-tier Enterprise AI-Augmented SDLC (A-SDLC) Framework coupling Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) policy guardrails, local context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), automated mutation test synthesis, and continuous AIOps observability. Finally, we analyze organizational governance imperatives, intellectual property licensing risks, and emerging horizons in autonomous multi-agent coding swarms, establishing an empirical blueprint for resilient, high-assurance software engineering.

Research Aim: This study aims to analyze the role of Artificial Intelligence in shaping inclusive leadership and to formulate strategies for strengthening local wisdom as a foundation for sustainable leadership. Design/Methods/Approach: The study employs a Literature Review approach, synthesizing scholarly works from Scopus, Web of Science, and Sinta (2010–2026). Thematic analysis is used to identify patterns and relationships among inclusive leadership, AI, and local wisdom. Research Finding: The findings reveal that inclusive leadership plays a critical role in bridging technological advancement and human values. It enhances employee engagement, innovation, and decision-making quality while mitigating algorithmic bias. Additionally, integrating local wisdom strengthens ethical governance, social legitimacy, and organizational sustainability through value-based and culturally grounded practices. Theoretical Contribution/Originality: This research offers a novel integrative framework combining AI, inclusive leadership, and local wisdom, addressing the gap between technological and humanistic perspectives in leadership studies. Practitioner/Policy Implication: The study provides strategic guidance for leaders and policymakers to implement human-centered AI, promote inclusivity, and embed cultural values into digital transformation. Research Limitation: This study relies on secondary data; future research should incorporate empirical validation and sector-specific analysis.

This paper develops a critical theoretical framework for understanding national Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategies through the lens of "Governance as Infrastructure." Integrating insights from Infrastructure Studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS), this paper employs Black Feminist Technoscience (BFTS) to reveal how AI governance infrastructures are assembled, maintained, and contested, and whose forms of knowledge, labour, and experience are rendered visible or invisible in these processes. We analyze the Canadian AI governance landscape through in-depth interviews with bureaucrats, civil society advocacy groups, academic researchers, and industry actors. Our inductive thematic analysis reveals how AI governance infrastructure enacts specific configurations of power, particularly through the politics of expertise; how actors navigate profound ambiguities related to AI's opacity, often involving strategic ignorance; and how mechanisms for justice and accountability struggle to address AI-related harms. We contend that a BFTS perspective highlights the limitations of current governance approaches and points toward alternative infrastructural designs prioritizing care, maintenance, participatory democracy, and adaptive temporalities to foster more equitable and accountable technology governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used across healthcare to analyze complex clinical data, support diagnosis, guide precision medicine, accelerate drug discovery, and enable remote monitoring. This review examines established AI/ML techniques and their current clinical and commercial applications while considering the requirements for trustworthy adoption. Evidence reviewed across medical imaging, electronic health records, drug discovery, precision medicine, and remote patient monitoring shows broad use of supervised, unsupervised, deep-learning, hybrid, and ensemble approaches. Reported benefits include improved diagnostic and predictive performance, earlier risk identification, and support for individualized treatment. Recurring barriers include data privacy, model opacity, computational demands, algorithmic bias, limited external validation, workflow integration, and workforce readiness. Explainable AI, privacy-preserving learning, human-in-the-loop oversight, and evolving regulatory frameworks are prominent responses to these challenges. AI/ML is moving from experimental development toward practical healthcare use, but dependable adoption requires more than predictive accuracy. Robust external validation, transparent and interpretable models, privacy protection, equitable datasets, appropriate regulation, and effective clinician-AI collaboration are central to building trustworthy clinical systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Beyond AI Sandboxes and Permission Checks: A Technical Specification for Cross-Platform AI Execution Finality, Hardware Security, and Interoperability New here? Download the presentation first for a quick visual overview, then the full specification. The problem AI agents no longer just generate text. They run code, call APIs, operate browsers, move money, and control devices across iOS, Android, desktop, cloud, and hardware. An agent can be sandboxed, logged in, and approved by a permission check, and still lack the authority to cause the specific effect it is about to cause, at the moment that effect occurs. Sandboxes limit where an agent runs. Permission checks approve categories of action. Neither binds authority to the actual operation presented at the point where it takes effect. The core idea Computation is not authority to act. The specification treats computing an action and making it effective as separate, independently verified steps: Candidate Act → Non-Effective State → Protected Validation → Scoped Finality Authority → Finality Sink Verification → Controlled Effectuation A proposed operation stays non-effective until an independent Finality Sink reconstructs the actual operation and verifies protected evidence and scoped, non-bearer, single-use authority. If any check fails, the effect does not happen. What the specification covers AI-agent security: tool execution, prompt-injection containment, external-action authorization iOS, Android, and cross-platform interoperability for third-party AI tools Agent gateways, sandbox egress, credential release, and non-bypassable enforcement Trusted execution environments, kernel mediation, virtualization, and hardware command boundaries Multi-agent delegation, causal dependencies, conflicting operations, and revocation Cloud, enterprise, financial, robotics, and safety-relevant systems The full document contains the detailed embodiments, definitions, workflows, and algorithms. Run it yourself: reference implementation with 400 automated tests https://github.com/sangmdas/ios-android-ai-execution-finality A vendor-neutral Python and SQLite reference model of the core workflow. All 400 tests pass. It demonstrates: the exact SHA-256 commitment of a Candidate Act and its Non-Effective State; operation-bound authority checks: principal, tenant, route, resource, quota, expiry, and generation; independent Finality Sink verification of the actual operation; single-use scoped authority and replay prevention; revocation and ownership epochs; atomic consumption, plus crash and lost-acknowledgement recovery; causal receipts between dependent operations. bash git clone https://github.com/sangmdas/ios-android-ai-execution-finality cd ios-android-ai-execution-finality python -m pip install -e . python -m pytest -q # 400 passed The model is platform-neutral. It does not include privileged iOS or Android system hooks, TEE or hardware enforcement, or cross-system atomic transactions. Those mechanisms are described in the specification. See docs/LIMITATIONS.md in the repository. Independent review is welcome through GitHub Issues and Discussions. The adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies presents significant opportunities to enhance occupational safety and health (OSH) management within modern methods of construction (MMC). However, organisations often lack clarity on which factors are crucial for the adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies for OSH improvement in MMC. Existing studies have mainly investigated individual technologies, adoption barriers, or organisational capability factors, without systematically identifying and prioritising the comprehensive set of people, organisational, technological, and infrastructure attributes that enable effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC. This study addresses this gap by identifying, validating, and prioritising the key attributes for effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC using a four-stage methodological approach comprising SLR, expert verification, Delphi method, and voting analytic hierarchy process (VAHP). Through a combination of systematic literature review (SLR) and expert verification, 21 attributes were identified and grouped into four clusters: people, organisation, technology, and infrastructure. The 21 identified and validated attributes were then ranked by a group of experts through a two-round Delphi survey. Following this, the weights and importance of attributes were determined using the voting analytical hierarchy process (VAHP). The results indicate that organisation and people clusters achieved the highest relative priorities; Management support, workforce competence, and technology acceptance were identified as the highest-priority attributes. These findings reveal a sociotechnical hierarchy in which organisational and human capabilities are prioritised above technological and infrastructural capabilities, suggesting successful Industry 4.0-enabled transformation for OSH improvement depends more on social-subsystem capability than on technology deployment alone.

Digital-based Islamic Religious Education (IRE) provides opportunities to use learning activity data to understand student engagement and learning outcomes. However, high levels of digital activity do not necessarily indicate deep cognitive engagement or successful learning. This study aims to analyze the use of learning analytics to examine student engagement and learning outcomes in digital-based IRE. It employs a qualitative approach using the library research method. Data were obtained by reviewing relevant literature on learning analytics, student engagement, learning outcomes, and digital-based IRE, and were analyzed descriptively through the identification and synthesis of findings. The results indicate that learning analytics can be used to identify behavioral engagement through access to learning materials, task completion, and participation in assessments, as well as to examine cognitive engagement through students’ understanding of learning materials and the quality of their responses. The use of these data can help educators identify learning difficulties, provide feedback, and determine appropriate instructional follow-up. Nevertheless, the relationship between engagement and learning outcomes must be interpreted cautiously because it is influenced by various factors. Digital activity data are also insufficient to assess all aspects of religious understanding and character development. This study concludes that learning analytics has the potential to support pedagogical decision-making in digital-based IRE, provided that data quality, privacy, and the learning context are taken into account.

The growing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into human cognitive activities, including problem-solving, decision-making, learning and information processing, has raised important questions about cognitive work allocation, metacognitive control and independent performance. Although GenAI can enhance efficiency by reducing cognitive demands, excessive reliance may weaken users’ engagement in reasoning, verification and independent task execution. This review examines the relationship between GenAI use and human cognition, with particular emphasis on cognitive offloading, appropriate reliance, over-reliance, automation bias and independent performance. Drawing on existing research, it explores how the effects of cognitive offloading depend on task characteristics and the distribution of cognitive responsibility between users and AI systems. The review further considers interventions such as think-first strategies, cognitive forcing functions, reflection, verification prompts and adaptive scaffolding that aim to preserve human cognitive engagement while benefiting from AI assistance. In addition, it examines behavioural telemetry including prompt intent, interaction timing, response editing and verification activities as a potential means of identifying patterns of engagement and reliance during multi-turn human AI interactions. These observable behaviours are treated as indirect indicators rather than definitive measures of internal cognitive processes. The review highlights the importance of evaluating not only task performance with AI assistance but also users’ ability to perform independently when such assistance is unavailable. It identifies a need for integrated frameworks that connect cognitive work allocation, metacognition, observable interaction patterns, reliance calibration and independent performance over time. Such frameworks may support the development of human-centred GenAI systems that improve task effectiveness while maintaining users’ critical thinking, self-regulation and cognitive autonomy.

documents.abstract: This study examined how students’ motivational regulation during creative writing was organized when generative artificial intelligence (AI) was unavailable or optionally available. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), motivation was conceptualized as configurations of intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, and external regulation. The sample comprised 406 students in Grades 5–8 who completed comparable creative writing tasks without AI (Time 1) and with optional AI access (Time 2). Using a micro-longitudinal, person-centered design, latent profile analyses identified motivational configurations and examined psychological need satisfaction and academic achievement as predictors of profile membership; degree of AI use was examined at Time 2. Mean levels of motivational regulation remained largely stable, whereas person-centered analyses revealed heterogeneity in regulatory configurations and differences in the prevalence of comparable profiles. Autonomy satisfaction declined at Time 2, while higher need satisfaction, particularly autonomy and competence, was associated with more self-determined configurations. End-of-term grades differentiated profile membership at both occasions. Degree of AI use did not significantly predict profile membership. Cross-context analyses showed correspondence alongside redistribution. Because full profile similarity was unsupported, these patterns were interpreted descriptively rather than as transitions between equivalent latent states. AI availability coincided with configurational differences not apparent from mean-level analyses. The findings distinguish AI availability from usage intensity and suggest that AI-supported writing should be understood in relation to psychological needs, academic functioning, and regulatory demands surrounding support, delegation, authorship, and agency.
